concept.name: Wyckoff Phase D
concept.definition: The fourth phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which demand (accumulation) or supply (distribution) becomes consistently dominant: advances widen in spread and volume while reactions shrink, carrying price at least to the range boundary. LPSs and LPSYs in this phase are the framework's preferred position-entry areas.
concept.intuition: The tug-of-war ends and one side visibly wins — rallies get stronger and pullbacks weaker (or vice versa) as price presses toward the range edge.
concept.mechanics: The analyst verifies the Phase C conclusion by observing the character of subsequent swings: in accumulation, signs of strength on widening spread and volume alternate with shallow, low-volume reactions (LPSs) as price moves to or through the top of the range; in distribution, signs of weakness alternate with feeble rallies (LPSYs) as price moves to or through support.
concept.failure_modes: The expected dominance can fail to materialize — price returns to mid-range and the phase labels must be revised; entering on an LPS/LPSY assumes Phase D is underway, which is only confirmed by later action.
concept.misconceptions: Phase D is not the same as the trend itself; the decisive exit from the range belongs to Phase E, and treating every approach to the range edge as a breakout invites losses on failed moves.
concept.example: After a spring, a stock makes two widening-spread rallies to the top of its range, each followed by shallow low-volume dips; the analyst buys the second dip (LPS) anticipating Phase E markup.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
citations.section: Accumulation: Wyckoff Phases (Phase D); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase D)
